1:
Why the chapter opens with a protest of affection is explained by everyone, and two of the explanations are unusually shrewd. Chrysostom sees a man about to rebuke more vehemently than before, clearing away suspicion of hatred first, and straining to find some shadow of an excuse for those he must accuse. Theodoret puts it more coolly: he mingles his censure with praise, hiding as it were the hook beneath a bait, so that the benefit of what he says may be accepted. Clarke notices the same structure, that the apology prepares them for harsher truths to come. Calvin adds a second motive: the love was genuine, but the teaching would never have been received by Jews who thought him hostile, and Gentiles would have suspected his defection. Barnes turns the verse on preachers — ministers have no pleasure in proclaiming that men must be lost, and even while declaring it may sincerely seek the salvation of those they warn; he calls the teaching he had himself been defending appalling.

The prayer itself is made an argument. Wesley says flatly that Paul would not have prayed thus had they been absolutely reprobated, and Robertson quotes Bengel to precisely the same effect, adding that Paul plainly did not think the case hopeless. Henry reads the wish as implying conviction and conversion, since none could pray in faith that they be saved in their unbelief — though the apostle preached against them, he prayed for them. On the word rendered desire, Ellicott and Barnes agree it means goodwill, while Robertson can find no papyrus instance bearing that sense at all. Ellicott adds a textual note: the true reading is for them, Israel having begun as a marginal gloss that found its way into the text.

On the zeal that is not according to knowledge, Ellicott documents the zeal generously before criticising it, quoting Josephus that a Jew knows the Law better than his own name, that Jews under Caligula died by fire and cross and prisoners of the last war by the claws of lions rather than sin against it — what Greek, he asks, would do the like? — and that proselytes filled Asia Minor and Syria and, to the indignation of Tacitus, Italy and Rome. Wesley compresses the whole verse into an epigram aimed at his own readers, that they had zeal without knowledge and we have knowledge without zeal.

Whether the ignorance excuses them then divides the commentators four ways. Clarke says they sinned more through ignorance than malice and that this pleads in their excuse. Calvin grants the same fact and destroys the plea with it: it is commonly thought a fit defence that a man meant no harm, and many will not seek the truth because they suppose whatever is done ignorantly with good intention is excusable — yet none of us would excuse the crucifixion of Christ, and those who did it had the very defence in which we confidently glory. Barnes draws the line differently: involuntary ignorance excuses from guilt, but ignorance produced by our own sin or indolence excuses no crime, and theirs was voluntary since they had full opportunity of knowing — though he allows it as mitigating, and holds that sincerity does not of itself constitute piety.

What righteousness of God means is the last question. Gill sets out three possibilities — the righteousness revealed in the gospel, the righteousness the law demands, or the attribute of divine justice — and prefers the last, they never conceiving God so strict as to weigh the heart's thoughts. Barnes denies exactly that: not the personal holiness of God, he says, but his plan of justifying men. Theodoret makes their own righteousness their unreasonable adherence to a law now ended, and Calvin makes the two righteousnesses contraries that cannot stand together, so that the first step toward God's is to renounce our own.
4:
One Greek word governs the passage, and the commentators divide three ways over it. Ellicott takes end in the sense of termination: Christ brings the functions of the law to an end by superseding it, and he quotes Bengel's picture of the law pursuing a man until he takes refuge in Christ, when it says, thou hast found thine asylum, I trouble thee no more. Clarke says the same in a sentence — where the law ends, Christ begins; the law ends with representative sacrifices and Christ begins with the real offering. Barnes and Wesley take it the other way, as design: the word can mean the object had in view, and Wesley makes it the very scope and aim of the law to bring men to believe. Theodoret agrees, denying any conflict — faith is not contrary to the law but most agreeable to it, since the law itself directed us to Christ, so that whoever trusts him fulfils its intention. Robertson and Calvin refuse to reduce the word at all. Robertson lists three things at once — Christ stopped the law as a means of salvation, is its goal, and is its fulfilment — judging the first the main idea here. Calvin sets out five senses with their references and rules that the meaning depends on what the word is joined to — the end of evils is their termination, of a promise its fulfilment, of a law its obedience, of faith salvation — then calls Christ the law's perfection, or its landing-place. Gill grants that Christ was the end of the ceremonial law in many respects, its final cause and substance and terminus, but denies this is chiefly meant.

The quotation from Moses then raises a real problem, and produces five solutions. The words in Deuteronomy were spoken of the law, and Paul applies them to faith. Calvin states the difficulty without softening it — the passage may not a little disturb the reader, seeming improperly applied and the words turned to another meaning — and unties it by arguing that if Moses meant the law only his reasoning would be frivolous, a law set before the eyes being no easier to keep than one far off. Ellicott concedes the original had quite a different application, referring to the very law the apostle depreciates, and holds the words are used allegorically. Robertson cuts it shorter: Paul takes phrases from the Greek version and uses them for his own conviction of the gospel, and does not quote Moses as saying this or meaning this. Barnes takes a middle course, that Moses nowhere describes justification by faith but did use language which fitly expresses it. Theodoret solves it by changing the speaker — not Moses himself, but the God of all through Moses, speaks thus.

Three of them note that the righteousness of faith is personified and made to speak. On the other side of the contrast, the man that doeth these things shall live in them, Wesley states the terms exactly: he alone may claim life who keeps every precept in every point, which makes the way impossible to any who has transgressed once. Clarke reaches the same by the curse pronounced on whoever continues not in all things written. Ellicott corrects the reading, that it is probably in it rather than by them, meaning the righteousness just named. Clarke offers a second sense for the question about ascending, that those refusing Christ crucified must in effect seek another Messiah with a different revelation; Cyril takes the descent into the deep as the resurrection and marshals the witnesses, so that whoever will not believe one has twelve, and whoever disbelieves the twelve may take the five hundred. Henry brings it to use: not Christ in heaven nor Christ in the deep is meant, but Christ in the promise, offered in the word.
7:
The second question is not what Moses wrote, and the closest readers all say so. The Hebrew asks who shall go over the sea; Paul asks who shall descend into the abyss. Barnes explains the original — crossing the Mediterranean was in early navigation an enterprise of the highest difficulty, and the regions beyond it were reckoned at a vast distance — and holds the words are changed but not the sense, the apostle professing not to quote Moses but to express the language of faith. Ellicott is blunter: the word does stand for the sea in the Greek version, but here means the abyss of Hades. Robertson agrees the reference is to the other world to which Christ went after death, and credits the change to art, saying Paul seizes on the words with an orator's instinct. Theodoret describes the same operation without embarrassment: God spoke those words concerning the law, teaching the Jews they had received without labour the knowledge of what to do; the apostle has transferred them to faith, and what Moses once said of the law's injunctions we now say of believing.

That the word is nigh is then read as comfort and as limit. Clarke takes the comfort — no occasion to seek high or low, the way being plain and the doctrine easy to understand and to profess. Calvin draws the contrast sharply: one righteousness shows itself at a distance and restrains men from coming near, while the other offers itself at hand and kindly invites us — but he adds a restriction, that the limits of the word are prescribed lest men be led away by crafts and wander from the way. Wesley says all is done ready to our hand; Barnes, that the doctrine was so familiar it was already their common conversation.

Confession and belief are then put in an order that troubles some of them. Calvin sees the difficulty: the regular order would put faith of the heart first and the confession arising from it second, and he offers two explanations — that the apostle follows the order in which Moses gave the words, and, from Pareus, that we know not faith otherwise than by profession. Robertson passes the problem by and simply lays down that faith precedes confession, of course. Ellicott dissolves it instead, observing that the next verse takes the form of Hebrew parallelism, in which balanced clauses are treated as equivalent to one another. He adds a claim of some weight, that this is the earliest formal confession of faith on record, the one in Acts not being genuine.

What is confessed carries the most force. Robertson notes that nearly all manuscripts give Jesus as Lord, records the variant of a few, and explains why the formula tests everyone using it: no Jew would say it who had not trusted Christ, since in the Greek Bible that title belongs to God, and no Gentile who had not stopped calling the emperor by it — the word was and is the touchstone of faith. Wesley makes the cost explicit in a clause, that the confession is required even in time of persecution, when it may send a man to the lions. Barnes defines the verb as speaking what agrees with what another maintains, so that profession is a public declaration of agreement with all God has declared. Ellicott gives the resurrection the cardinal place: though the death of Christ is more especially the cause of salvation, without the resurrection the proof of his Messiahship would be incomplete and his death would lack its saving efficacy. Gill requires the confession to be hearty and public and to arise from experience of grace; Clarke reduces it to depending solely on him who died for our offences and rose for our justification; and Cyril gathers the texts that place Christ at the right hand of God.
10:
The verse restores the order the previous one inverted, as Robertson notes, putting faith before confession. Calvin observes that both verbs are impersonal — it is believed, it is confessed — and reports two judgments on the pairing. Pareus: God knows our faith, but it is made known to man by confession. Turrettin, more radically: the apostle loved antitheses, and faith and confession are not to be separated and assigned each its own result, but taken together, as when Christ is said to have been delivered for our offences and raised for our justification. Wesley takes exactly the division Turrettin denies: believing obtains justification and confessing final salvation, confession being the whole of outward religion as believing is the root of all inward. Theodoret keeps both without dividing them, requiring a firm faith and a bold confession, that the heart may be adorned with persuasion and the tongue dignified with proclamation.

What sort of believing is meant is then filled out. Gill says at length what it is not — not bare assent, not notional knowledge, not a man's saying he believes, lying neither in the brain nor the tongue — before saying what it is: heart work in which understanding and will and affections are all engaged, a seeing of the Son, a going out of the soul to Christ that ventures into his presence and prostrates itself there. Barnes puts it shorter, that no faith is genuine which does not influence the whole mind. Clarke has the heart duly affected with a sense of guilt and of the sufficiency of the sacrifice, and adds that a grand object throughout is to show the simplicity of the gospel together with its efficacy, being unlike a law full of rites.

The quotation that follows turns on a single added word, and three of them notice it independently. The prophet says indefinitely that he who believes shall not be ashamed; Robertson observes that Paul adds every one, Gill that where the prophet is indefinite an universal is used, and Calvin that the apostle hoists an universal banner and then extends it expressly to the Gentiles. Calvin also explains why the Greek version has ashamed where the Hebrew has make haste: he who hastens acts for the most part foolishly and brings himself to shame, as Saul did when he would not wait.

That there is no difference is then established from the character of God rather than from the condition of men. Henry states it plainly: there is not one God to the Jews who is more kind and another to the Gentiles who is less kind, but he is the same to all, a common father of mankind. Calvin argues from creation, that the Maker of the world is God of all men and will show himself kind to everyone who calls on him, since infinite mercy cannot but extend to all who seek it; and glosses rich as bountiful. Barnes qualifies: the absence of difference holds for the matter under discussion — in other respects a difference might remain, but not in the way of justification, since all had sinned and all must be justified alike. Ellicott corrects the construction, so that the words over all belong to the Lord rather than to the riches, and takes that Lord to be Christ, who is Lord of Jew and Gentile alike. Wesley presses the repetition furthest: the truth is stated, repeated here, repeated again and then confirmed, which he takes to imply not only that whoever calls shall be saved but that God wills all to call savingly upon him. Theodoret and Clarke agree in the plainest terms that all are equally welcome, one simple way being proposed to everyone.
13:
That the promise to whoever calls on the name of the Lord is here applied to Christ is agreed, and Barnes states its weight: this is one of many instances where the writers of the New Testament apply to him expressions belonging in the Old to God. Ellicott says the same more briefly, that the phrase originally meant Jehovah and is here referred to our Lord. Cyril presses the theophany where the Lord proclaims the name of the Lord, and asks: being himself the Lord, what Lord does he proclaim? — teaching covertly, he says, the doctrine of Father and Son. Theodoret notices something nobody else does, that the two quotations are fitted to the two organs of the preceding verses: to the heart, whoever believes shall not be ashamed; to the tongue, whoever calls shall be saved.

The chain of questions that follows is read five different ways. Chrysostom takes it as objection and answer, the whole passage framed out of them to convict his hearers and take from them every excuse, showing they were punishable for the ignorance itself. Barnes reconstructs the objection in the same spirit and gives it to a Jew: the plan makes salvation depend on faith, when a large part of the nation had never heard. Clarke reads it the other way round, as a ladder laid down in beautifully graduated order — no salvation without the gospel, no gospel without preaching, no effectual preaching without a divine mission, no benefit unless it is heard. Theodoret observes the order runs backwards: what is first in time, the sending of preachers, is put last, since appointment must precede preaching, preaching hearing, hearing belief — and adds that positions laid down as if to vindicate the Jews in fact increase their blame. Robertson sees Paul picking up each preceding verb to challenge it, and calls the result a powerful plea for missions. Calvin finds a personal stake: the calling of the Gentiles and Paul's own ministry stood or fell together, so he must prove the one and give a reason for the other, lest he seem to extend God's favour without authority and give the children's bread to dogs.

On the necessity of being sent, Gill divides the mission in two: the extraordinary kind the apostles had, with gifts and miracles and an immediate commission from Christ, and the ordinary call of pastors, which includes an inward call by the Spirit — one that does not arise, he is careful to say, from vanity of mind or desire of applause. Barnes notes the Jews themselves admitted the principle, since he who sends a message alone appoints who shall bear it. Calvin declines the whole question as beside the apostle's purpose here, and gives instead the sentence that carries the argument: the gospel does not fall like rain from the clouds, but is brought by the hands of men wherever it is sent from above. He adds that a nation favoured with the preaching has in that very fact a proof and pledge of divine love.

The beautiful feet are then variously accounted for. Clarke reports a suggestion that feet in scripture stand for things internal, the principles a man acts on, so that the feet of these messengers signify the validity of their mission and the authority on which they act. Wesley keeps them literal — their very footsteps, their coming. Robertson observes that the quotation follows the Hebrew more closely than the Greek and pictured the messengers of the return from captivity, the apostle assuming his own missionaries have been sent. Ellicott adds a textual correction, that the words about preaching the gospel of peace are absent from the oldest manuscripts and should be struck out, the quotation not being given in full.
16:
Two commentators notice the argument stops running straight here, and repair it differently. Barnes confesses the difficulty — it is not easy to see the connexion, and it has been questioned whether the sixteenth verse continues the objection or begins the answer — and after all the attention he can give it decides for an admission by the apostle. Then he does something more drastic with the next verse: the words that faith comes by hearing are, he takes it, the objector's own, turning the quotation from Isaiah back on Paul. If a report was necessary, men cannot be condemned for not obeying what never reached them, and salvation depends on a condition God himself put beyond their power. Ellicott finds the same untidiness and explains it as interleaving: the apostle has two thoughts at once, the necessity of preaching before believing and the refusal of the Jews to accept what was preached, and begins the second before finishing the first, so the seventeenth verse reaches back to the fifteenth while the sixteenth anticipates the nineteenth. Everyone else takes the verse as the apostle's own conclusion drawn from what precedes.

Calvin uses the sixteenth verse to block an inference. If faith always followed the word as corn follows seed, Israel, who had never been without the word, might make a boast of it; so the apostle intimates in passing that many are called who are yet not chosen. On the efficacy of preaching he is emphatic and careful at once: the passage testifies that faith is produced by preaching — yet of itself preaching avails nothing, becoming the instrument of God's power only when it pleases him to work, for the voice of man cannot penetrate the soul, and mortal man would be too much exalted if he could regenerate us. Clarke states the contrary as plainly: God brings the message but does not oblige men to embrace it, and it saves only if affectionately credited. Wesley inserts a guarding word — faith ordinarily comes by hearing — and Gill calls preachers instruments only.

Ellicott points out that the word rendered report in one verse and hearing in the next is the same, involving both preacher and hearer in the first place and only the hearer in the second. He and Robertson agree the text should read the word of Christ rather than of God, Robertson adding that the genitive is objective: the word about Christ.

The boldest stroke is the use of the psalm about the heavens declaring the glory of God, handled with varying frankness. Calvin admits it seems to bear little on the subject, the prophet speaking of the material works of God and not of apostles. Ellicott says the same in a line: the sound is here the preachers' voice and in the original the unspoken testimony of the heavenly bodies. Clarke makes the analogy carry the weight: as the luminaries testified of the eternal power and Godhead to the habitable world, so the gospel has testified through Palestine and the whole Roman empire. Wesley hedges with two words, that he may in some sense say of the preachers what David said of the lights of heaven. Theodoret argues from the order of the mission — how could the Jews not have heard, when the nations of the whole earth had heard and the preachers came to them first? Cyril turns on the objectors with much less restraint, telling them to read Lamentations, where Jeremiah wrote what was worthy of lamentation over them, and setting believing Persians against unbelieving Hebrews. Henry ends where the patience of God ends: it is called a day, fit for work, but limited as a day, with a night at the end — and we may wonder at a mercy not overcome by man's badness as much as at a badness not overcome by God's goodness.
19:
What Israel is asked whether they knew has to be supplied, and Barnes says so: the apostle does not state it, and it must be gathered from what follows — that the gospel was to go to the Gentiles and the Jews be cast off. Gill settles on the same answer, allowing they knew God and the gospel nationally and speculatively rather than spiritually, and rejected it against their own conviction. Calvin turns the question into an objection from the less to the greater: how comes it that aliens should run to a light shown from afar, while the race of Abraham rejects it seen at home?

The prophecy of jealousy is read by three of them as an exact requital. Clarke states the symmetry — as you provoked me with those that are no gods, I will provoke you by those that are no people — and Robertson and Wesley put it the same way independently. Ellicott explains the terms as Jewish usage about their neighbours, no people because they stood in no recognised relation to God and foolish because they had no special revelation. Theodoret does what none of the others do — takes the insult to himself. It is we, he says, whom the prophet called foolish, pointing to the folly we laboured under before conversion — and quotes the apostle's confession that we ourselves were sometime foolish and disobedient. He adds that neither captivity nor dispersion nor the loss of the temple has distressed them as the eminence of the Gentiles has. On the word first, Robertson and Ellicott agree it means earliest in time and in scripture.

That Isaiah is very bold is taken by nearly all as courage in the face of danger. Barnes glosses the verb as daring, the danger lying in avowing that the Jews would be cast off; Clarke has him speaking out among a perverse people; Gill says he risked his life; Theodoret that he feared not the murdering Jews; and Robertson that the apostle cites the passage in support of his own courage. Calvin alone reads the boldness as plainness rather than bravery: the prophet spoke neither figuratively nor with hesitation, but declared the calling of the Gentiles in plain words.

The last two verses raise a difficulty Ellicott states without flinching, twice. The words applied here to the Gentiles, he says, referred in the original to apostate Israel; and those that follow come from the very next verse of the same prophet, where no such distinction between the persons addressed is drawn. Calvin sees the same adjacency and turns it the other way: what Paul separated by interposing a few words stands connected in Isaiah, where the Lord declares he will turn his favour to the Gentiles and immediately subjoins the reason, that he was wearied by the perverseness of Israel — the two sentences being reversed in the citation. Clarke lets the nearness strengthen the case: the unbelief of the Jews was their own obstinacy, was foretold seven hundred years before, and so far from proving the gospel insufficient proves it the means God had provided.

On the stretched-out hands Calvin finds two ways by which God calls men, inviting by his word and alluring by every kindness, so that contempt of his truth is the more abominable for the solicitude refused. Barnes takes the gesture as entreaty and reads all day long to mean rebellion was the settled character of the people; Theodoret says it means without ceasing, on the authority of two Greek versions. Cyril reads the verse into the passion, setting the purple robe of the trial beside the prophet's question who is this that comes from Edom with garments red. Wesley closes by matching the chapter's ends: an unbelieving and gainsaying people are just the opposite of those who believe with the heart and confess with the mouth.
